title: 2105.09506v1
universal_lens: PINNs unify fluid dynamics PDEs with neural networks via automatic differentiation, enabling seamless data-model integration without mesh generation. The universal lens unifies partial differential equations and sparse observational data into a single variational optimization problem. By embedding physical conservation laws as soft constraints within the loss landscape, it establishes an isomorphism between solving complex continuum mechanics and minimizing a high-dimensional non-convex functional.
gsi_mapping: GSI employs Bayesian inference to calibrate PINN-derived posterior distributions over flow fields, enabling robust uncertainty quantification for real-time tactical decision-making. GSI maps this physics-informed framework to Bayesian inverse problems. Sparse sensor arrays (e.g., optical tracking) provide noisy likelihoods, while biomechanical and fluid-dynamic priors act as regularization. Conformal prediction intervals are derived from the residual variances of the neural network's PDE satisfaction.
gse_mapping: GSE utilizes PINN state transitions to model dynamic flow evolution, supporting situational awareness through continuous belief updates on boundary conditions and material properties. GSE utilizes these primitives for real-time situational reasoning. The continuous state-transition model infers hidden player states and momentum vectors from incomplete visual feeds. This allows the engine to predict trajectory evolutions and collision probabilities by strictly adhering to underlying Newtonian and aerodynamic constraints.

primitives.name: Inverse Flow Solver
primitives.verbatim_quote: Moreover, solving inverse flow problems is often prohibitively expensive and requires complex and expensive formulations and new computer codes.
primitives.assumptions: Inverse problems require costly reformulations; traditional methods demand specialized algorithms.
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-dimensional parameter estimation under noisy data constraints.

layer2.mapping: Maps inverse problem formulation to PINN loss landscape optimization, enabling simultaneous solution of PDEs and unknown parameters.
layer2.telemetry: Residual error convergence across spatio-temporal data points.

primitives.name: Meshless Physics-Informed Network
primitives.verbatim_quote: PINNs use automatic differentiation to represent all the differential operators and hence there is no explicit need for a mesh generation.
primitives.assumptions: Automatic differentiation replaces finite element discretization; no structured grid required.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Discrete derivative approximation in high-dimensional domains.

layer2.mapping: Derives governing equation residuals directly from neural network outputs using AD, bypassing mesh dependency.
layer2.telemetry: Gradient-based loss minimization performance relative to structured solvers.

primitives.name: Multifidelity Data Integration
primitives.verbatim_quote: Physics-informed learning [7], introduced in a series of papers by Karniadakis's group both for Gaussian-process regression [8,9] and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [10], can seamlessly integrate multifidelity/multimodality experimental data with the various Navier-Stokes formulations for incompressible flows [11,12] as well as compressible flows [13] and biomedical flows [14].
primitives.assumptions: Data fidelity levels vary; integration assumes compatible physical models.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Noise-tolerant fusion of disparate data sources into unified PDE framework.

layer2.mapping: Aligns heterogeneous data modalities within a common PINN architecture, enabling cross-scale inference.
layer2.telemetry: Cross-validation accuracy between low/high fidelity datasets.

primitives.name: Forward-Inverse Equivalence Principle
primitives.verbatim_quote: Moreover, the forward and inverse PINN formulations are identical so there is no need for expensive data assimilation schemes that have stalled progress especially for optimization and design applications of flow problems in the past.
primitives.assumptions: Formulation symmetry allows shared computational infrastructure for forward and inverse tasks.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Computational equivalence between deterministic and probabilistic flow inference.

layer2.mapping: Enables unified training protocol for both forward prediction and inverse parameter recovery.
layer2.telemetry: Training efficiency gain from shared architecture vs. separate assimilation pipelines.

primitives.name: Unified Forward-Inverse Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: 1) can be used for both forward and inverse problems.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: u: velocity field (m/s), p: pressure (Pa), x: spatial coordinates (m). All dimensionless in normalized PINN inputs.
primitives.assumptions: The governing Navier-Stokes equations hold; the solution space is sufficiently smooth to be approximated by a deep neural network.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down at extremely high Reynolds numbers where multi-scale turbulence requires prohibitive network depths, or when data noise overwhelms the physics residuals.

layer2.mapping: Maps the joint minimization of data mismatch and PDE residuals directly to GSI's joint posterior inference over latent kinematic states and physical parameters.
layer2.telemetry: Relative L2-norm error of reconstructed velocity and pressure fields compared to high-fidelity spectral element ground truth.

primitives.name: Physics-Data Fusion Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: Compared to the traditional CFD solvers, PINNs are superior at integrating the data (observations of the flow quantities) and physics (governing equations).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: L: total loss function (dimensionless), \lambda: weighting coefficients (dimensionless).
primitives.assumptions: Observational data is unbiased but sparse; the physics equations accurately describe the macroscopic behavior of the system.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails if the underlying physics model is fundamentally incorrect for the regime (e.g., ignoring compressibility in supersonic flows).

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSE's sensor fusion module, combining discrete tracking data with continuous biomechanical constraints to resolve occluded athlete positions.
layer2.telemetry: Reduction in reconstruction error relative to purely data-driven autoencoders lacking PDE constraints.

primitives.name: Visual Field Inverter
primitives.verbatim_quote: A promising application is on the flow visualization technology [12,51], where the flow fields can be easily inferred from the observations such as concentration fields and images.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: C: concentration field (kg/m^3), I: image intensity (dimensionless pixels).
primitives.assumptions: There exists a differentiable mapping between the observed scalar fields/images and the underlying vector velocity fields.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Ill-posed when the observation operator lacks sensitivity to certain flow modes (e.g., inferring 3D vorticity from a single 2D projection without symmetry assumptions).

layer2.mapping: Directly maps to GSI's computer vision pipeline, inferring full 3D player kinematics and ball trajectories from 2D broadcast camera feeds.
layer2.telemetry: Pixel-wise MSE between inferred and ground-truth scalar fields, coupled with divergence-free constraint violations.

primitives.name: Sparse Volumetric Reconstructor
primitives.verbatim_quote: In particular, we apply PINNs to reconstruct the 3D flow fields based on a few two-dimensional and two-component (2D2C) velocity observations.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: u_{2D2C}: observed 2D velocity components (m/s), V_{3D}: full 3D volumetric field (m/s).
primitives.assumptions: The unobserved dimensions are strongly correlated with the observed planes via the continuity and momentum equations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Regime of extreme sparsity where the number of observed planes is insufficient to constrain the highest frequency turbulent eddies.

layer2.mapping: Mirrors GSE's capability to reconstruct full team formations and off-ball movements using only limited tracking data from specific zones of the pitch.
layer2.telemetry: Volumetric correlation coefficient between reconstructed and true 3D velocity fields across varying degrees of observational sparsity.

primitives.name: Physics-Informed Neural Network Inference Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: 5: Case study of PINNs for incompressible flows: inference result of PINNs for Case 2.
primitives.assumptions: Neural network approximates solution to PDEs with minimal boundary condition specification; data constraints guide training via residual loss.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When boundary conditions are unknown or inaccessible, PINNs rely on interior residuals and global constraints for inference.

layer2.mapping: Maps PDE solution space to probabilistic latent manifold via stochastic gradient descent with physics-informed loss function.
layer2.telemetry: Residual error norm and convergence rate of trained network against reference CFD data.

primitives.name: Shock Wave Boundary Condition Approximation
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, for the shock wave problem in high-speed flows, the boundary conditions in real experiments are usually not known and can only be estimated approximately.
primitives.assumptions: Real-world boundary conditions are imprecise; approximate estimation allows for viable PINN formulation without full specification.
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-speed compressible flows where experimental boundary data is unavailable or unreliable.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphically maps real-world noisy boundary estimates to synthetic training targets via augmented Lagrangian regularization.
layer2.telemetry: Relative deviation of predicted shock structure from known CFD benchmarks under varying boundary approximations.

primitives.name: Density Gradient Constraint
primitives.verbatim_quote: Note that unlike the one-dimensional case, where the density gradient in the whole computational domain is used in [13], here we only use the density gradients in a sub-domain D of the computational domain Ω, i.e., D ⊂Ω.
primitives.assumptions: Local density gradient information suffices for accurate reconstruction; global domain coverage is unnecessary.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When full domain gradient data is computationally prohibitive or experimentally inaccessible.

layer2.mapping: Derives local PDE residuals from subset of domain gradients, enabling localized PINN training with reduced data footprint.
layer2.telemetry: Mean squared error between PINN-predicted and measured density gradients within subdomain D.

primitives.name: Global Physical Constraints
primitives.verbatim_quote: 8 using PINNs based on the data of density gradients ∇ρ motivated by the Schlieren photography available experimentally; additionally, we use limited data of the surface pressure obtained by pressure sensors as well as the global constrains (mass, momentum and energy).
primitives.assumptions: Global conservation laws provide sufficient structure to regularize underdetermined inverse problems in fluid mechanics.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sparse observational data combined with known macroscopic conservation principles.

layer2.mapping: Embeds mass, momentum, and energy conservation into PINN loss landscape as soft equality constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Deviation from conservation law integrals computed over entire domain during PINN optimization.

primitives.name: Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The goal is to infer the unknown permeability (for the shell and core) and velocity field based on the measurable phase field data.
primitives.assumptions: The underlying fluid dynamics are governed by the Navier-Stokes equations, and the permeability distribution within the thrombus is assumed to be spatially varying but constant in time. The phase field variable φ represents the local microstructure, distinguishing between the impermeable core and permeable shell.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the phase field transitions sharply across the core-shell interface, the inferred permeability κ(φ) becomes highly nonlinear, leading to potential numerical instability in the PINN training. Additionally, if the measurement noise exceeds a certain threshold, the Bayesian posterior distribution may become multimodal, making the inference problem ill-posed.

layer2.mapping: The PINN framework for inferring heterogeneous permeability fields is directly analogous to the Galaxy Sports Intelligence (GSI) task of learning latent player states and tactical embeddings from multi-resolution observational data. Both involve solving an inverse problem where the hidden state (permeability field or player embedding) is reconstructed from indirect measurements (phase field evolution or game trajectories). The Bayesian uncertainty quantification in PINNs maps to conformal predictive sets in GSI, providing probabilistic guarantees for predictions.
layer2.telemetry: The history of network losses (Loss PDE, Loss IC, Loss BC, Loss Data) serves as a verification metric, similar to how cross-validation loss curves are monitored in GSI models to detect overfitting.

primitives.name: Phase-Dependent Permeability Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: The core permeability is 0.001 and the shell permeability is set 1 as the actual values.
primitives.assumptions: The permeability κ is modeled as a function of the phase field variable κ(φ). Within the core (φ ≈ 0), κ approaches a small value (0.001), while in the shell (φ ≈ 1), κ is approximately 1. This piecewise behavior captures the stark contrast in fluid resistance between the solid clot and the loosely-packed platelet layer.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the inferred permeability κ(φ) fails to capture the sharp transition at the interface, the resulting velocity field will exhibit artificial smoothing, violating mass conservation. Furthermore, when the ratio of core-to-shell permeability is extremely large (> 1000), the stiffness of the governing equations can cause gradient-based optimization to stall.

layer2.mapping: The phase-dependent permeability model mirrors the concept of adaptive weighting matrices in Galaxy Sports Engine (GSE) state-transition models. Here, κ(φ) acts as a gating mechanism that modulates the influence of different regions (core vs. shell) on the overall flow dynamics, analogous to how GSE uses attention mechanisms to weigh the importance of various tactical contexts during a match.
layer2.telemetry: The inferred parameters a = 7.10 and b = 0.0003 from Figure 9(b) provide a direct calibration metric for the sigmoidal fit κ(φ) = 1/(1 + exp(-a*(φ-b))), ensuring that the model accurately reproduces the prescribed physical values.

primitives.name: Data-Assisted Learning Paradigm
primitives.verbatim_quote: 10,000 data points are scattered in the spatio-temporal domain from 30 snapshots (t ∈[0.03,0.93]) as the training data to infer the permeability.
primitives.assumptions: The dataset consists of sparse, noisy measurements of the phase field φ(x,t) and velocity u(x,t) at discrete times. The temporal resolution is sufficient to capture the evolution of the thrombus morphology, while the spatial distribution ensures adequate coverage of both the core and shell regions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: With only 10,000 data points, the empirical risk minimization may suffer from underfitting if the underlying manifold is too complex. Conversely, if the data contains systematic biases (e.g., clustering around the interface), the learned permeability map could be systematically distorted, leading to poor generalization to unseen timeslices.

layer2.mapping: The data-assisted learning paradigm aligns with the Galaxy Sports Engine's (GSE) approach to learn state-transition kernels from event logs. In both cases, a limited set of high-dimensional observations (phase field/trajectory) is used to calibrate a lower-dimensional latent representation (permeability field/embedding). The stochastic sampling strategy employed here is akin to mini-batch training in GSE, where only a subset of recent game events is used per update to enable online adaptation.
layer2.telemetry: The distribution of training points (1,000 initial, 10,000 interior, 1,000 boundary) provides a diagnostic tool for assessing the representativeness of the dataset, similar to how GSI evaluates the diversity of its input features to avoid over-reliance on specific scenarios.

primitives.name: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
primitives.verbatim_quote: We draw 1,000 points from an initial snapshot, 10,000 inner points to compute the PDE residuals, and 1,000 boundary points to compute the residuals at boundaries.
primitives.assumptions: The measurement errors are independent and identically distributed Gaussian noise with zero mean. The prior distribution over the network weights is chosen to be isotropic Gaussian, inducing a regularization effect that prevents overfitting to the sparse data.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the noise variance is underestimated, the posterior distribution becomes overly confident, leading to overconfident predictions that do not account for model misspecification. Conversely, if the noise is overestimated, the uncertainty intervals become excessively wide, reducing the utility of the probabilistic estimates.

layer2.mapping: Bayesian uncertainty quantification in PINNs corresponds to the conformal prediction framework used in Galaxy Sports Intelligence (GSI) for generating reliable betting margins. Both methods provide rigorous coverage guarantees by accounting for epistemic uncertainty. In GSI, the conformal set is updated sequentially as new market data arrives, mirroring the iterative refinement of posterior distributions in PINNs through additional data.
layer2.telemetry: The comparison of phase field and velocity field in Figure 9(c) along with their absolute error serves as a direct measure of predictive uncertainty, analogous to the confidence intervals produced by GSI models for outcome probabilities.

The chapter window delineates the transition from classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for solving incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. The core mathematical doctrine here is the reformulation of boundary value problems as unconstrained optimization tasks. Instead of discretizing the domain into a mesh (as done by the spectral/hp element method in Nektar), PINNs employ a collocation method where a fully-connected neural network acts as the trial solution. The loss function aggregates the mean squared error of the PDE residuals (continuity and momentum) evaluated at randomly sampled collocation points, alongside boundary condition violations and data mismatches. 

This approach inherently bridges forward simulations and inverse reconstructions. In the context of the cited case study, the inverse problem involves recovering a complete 3D velocity and pressure field from severely undersampled 2D2C planar observations. Mathematically, this is an ill-posed interpolation problem that becomes well-posed through the imposition of the Navier-Stokes operators as hard or soft constraints. The use of the sine activation function ($\sigma = \sin(\cdot)$) is particularly notable, as it aligns with the spectral bias required to approximate oscillatory fluid dynamics efficiently. For Galaxy Sports Intelligence, this doctrinal shift implies that we do not need exhaustive tracking data; by embedding the 'physics' of player motion and ball aerodynamics into our neural architectures, we can robustly infer hidden states from sparse, noisy optical observations, mirroring the 3D reconstruction from 2D slices.

It evolves from classical collocation methods and radial basis function approximations but leverages modern deep learning optimizers like ADAM. Historically, it represents a departure from grid-based finite volume/element methods, echoing the early 20th-century desire for meshless solutions but empowered by contemporary GPU-accelerated automatic differentiation.
